an1.209:1.1: Rāhula was the Buddha’s son to his wife Bhaddakaccānā ([an1.245]()). Rāhula’s going forth is related at [pli-tv-kd1:54.1.1](), and other important discourses with him include [mn61](), [mn62](), and [mn147]() = [sn35.121](). In the latter he became an arahant, which he confirmed in his own words at [thag4.8](). Commentaries explain his name as meaning “bondage”, but it probably refers rather to being born under the influence of the dark star Rāhu ([sn2.8]()). His desire for training is illustrated in a series of lessons through which Rāhula doggedly persists ([sn18.1]()). His death is not noted in the early texts.
an1.210:1.1: The story of Raṭṭhapāla, the “guardian of the nation”, has become one of the most famous and beloved parables from early Buddhism ([mn82]()). It is a testament to a young man’s resolution to go forth out of faith. His verses are at [thag16.4]().
an1.211:1.1: Kuṇḍadhāna has a single verse, which however has nothing to do with this subject ([thag1.15]()), and he may be listed along with Sakyan monks at [mn68:2.2.](). It is not clear why he has this honor. The commentarial story is absurd, and it seems the true context is lost. | Saṅgha procedures normally require consensus from the community that is present. In certain situations, however, a vote may be performed. Votes were tallied by distributing “ballot slips” (_salāka_). The one who manages the process must be of exemplary character ([pli-tv-kd14:9.1.1]()).
an1.212:1.1: Vaṅgīsa, the finest poet of the Saṅgha, is featured in [sn8.1]()–12, which provide prose settings for his Theragāthā verses at [thag21.1]().
an1.213:1.1: Upasena son of Vaṅgantā was said to be Sāriputta’s younger brother. When newly ordained, he made the mistake of ordaining students too early ([pli-tv-kd1:31.3.2]()), but later developed an impressive following ([pli-tv-bu-vb-np15:1.1.9]()), leading the Buddha to declare him the foremost of those who were “impressive all around”. His song of triumph is recorded at [ud4.9](), while his verses at [thag10.6]() focus on contentment and humility. He died of snakebite ([sn35.69]()). | The topic of one who is “impressive all around” is discussed at [an5.162](), [an8.71]()–2, and [an10.8]()–10. It was later used as the name of the Vinaya commentary, Samantapāsādika.
an1.214:1.1: Dabba was awakened at age seven, and the background for his service to the Saṅgha is recounted in the Vinaya ([pli-tv-bu-vb-ss8]() = [pli-tv-kd14:4.1.2]()). It did not make him popular in certain circles ([pli-tv-bu-vb-ss9](), [pli-tv-kd15:20.1.1]()), so here the Buddha acclaims his life dedicated to selfless public service. His spectacular demise is told at [ud8.9](). His singular verse puns on his name ([thag1.5]()).
an1.215:1.1: His verses are at [thag1.9](), and a personality quirk is discussed at [ud3.6](). But he is most remembered for his stories in the Vinaya, where he was said to have gifted a child with a miraculous golden garland ([pli-tv-bu-vb-np23]() = [pli-tv-kd6:15.1.1]()); these chapters also tell of his various medical troubles. One time, he was said to have saved children from kidnappers ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pj2:7.47.1]()). None of these contexts, however, clarify why he received this particular honor.
an1.216:1.1: Having previously gone forth in another religion, he sought out the Buddha while on almsround. He quickly realized perfection, but died soon after ([ud1.10]()).
an1.217:1.1: “Kassapa the Prince” (Kumārakassapa) was ordained at twenty ([pli-tv-kd1:75.1.1]()). He features in the Pāyāsisutta ([dn23]()), the Vammikasutta ([mn23]()), and his verses are collected in the Theragāthā ([thag2.41]()). His distinction here is apparently in recognition of the rhetorical skills displayed in the Pāyāsisutta. Since that sutta begins without mentioning the Buddha, however, it was probably spoken after the Buddha’s passing (see commentary to Vimānavatthu 74), so his inclusion here must have been later still.
an1.218:1.1: Mahākoṭṭhita was skill in the “methods of textual analysis” (_paṭisambhidā_) is  exemplified by such discussions as [mn43]() and [sn12.67](). His verse is at [thag1.2:0.4](). | For more on the topic, see [an4.172]().
